prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its translation into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B041 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The argument is that the chain from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect in humans, through GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, to a drug class with documented outcome benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity and now cardiovascular and renal disease is unusually complete and has been confirmed independently in large randomized trials. Holst and Drucker carry the physiology and the therapeutic rationale. Knudsen carries the step that made it a medicine: the protraction chemistry behind liraglutide and semaglutide. I keep Knudsen in the trio because a prize that credits only hormone biology would leave out the reason the discovery changed practice. The citation is worded around physiology and its translation so that it fits the three names.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and a three-person limit forces an exclusion that some will read as unjust. Mojsov's characterization of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide form is contested, and Habener is not on our list at all. There is also a structural tension: two of the three names are physiologists and one is an industrial drug developer, and a reader could say the citation merges two different achievements. If the committee decides that the basic strand and the drug-design strand deserve separate recognition, the configuration should be reconsidered. Because B041 has so much first-round support, we should also check that it is not simply the most obvious name on the list.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treating Mojsov's identification of the active peptide form as the stronger scientific third name, with Knudsen as a plausible alternative.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov point seriously and I do not think the supplied text settles priority for GLP-1(7-36). My difficulty is that peptide identification alone was not what turned the hormone into a therapy. The native peptide's short half-life was the obstacle, and the long-acting analogues removed it. For that reason I would rather credit the drug-development step than the identification step. I would revisit this if colleagues can show that Mojsov's contribution was the necessary enabling step and not one of several parallel ones. Without that, I do not think a third slot can be justified on the strength of a contested priority claim.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks CAR-T second but would credit only June and Sadelain, treating Rosenberg as a foundational predecessor and not a direct contributor.
responses.response: I disagree partly. I included Rosenberg in my own CAR-T trio because adoptive cell transfer and the early gene-modified T-cell trials are part of why the approach was clinically testable. I accept that his work is more distant from CAR design than June's and Sadelain's, and that a two-person CAR-T award is cleaner. This matters for my alternatives because it affects whether B035 can stand as a fallback, and I would not insist on the third name there. Eshhar's absence from the credited list is the more serious weakness of B035, and it applies whichever of us is right about Rosenberg.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks optogenetics second, as a broadly enabling method that transformed causal neuroscience, and accepts that any trio from six credited names is contestable.
responses.response: I agree optogenetics is a method with unusual reach, and I ranked it third myself. My reservation is that the case is mainly a research-tool one, since clinical use is limited to early vision-restoration work. Whether the prize criterion is met as strongly as for a therapy is a judgment, and I do not think it should be decided by the neuroscientists among us because it is familiar to us. I also think the molecular discoverers (Nagel, Hegemann) and the neuronal demonstrators (Deisseroth, Boyden) are different strands, and leaving out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck would make the configuration the hardest to defend of those we are discussing. I therefore see B033 as a credible alternative, not a rival to B041.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks BCR-ABL inhibition second, with a clean attribution among Lydon (compound), Druker (proof) and Sawyers (resistance), and notes that the case is mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: The BCR-ABL case is strong on clarity of credit and on maturity, which is better than what I can say for most of the field. I ranked it sixth because the paradigm of targeted kinase inhibition is already widely absorbed into oncology and is partly recognized through earlier prizes for related ideas, so the marginal conceptual novelty seems lower to me than for CAR-T. I would not want us to dismiss it. If the committee wants a configuration with minimal attribution dispute, it is the best offer, and I would like to hear whether you think Sawyers belongs on equal footing with Lydon and Druker.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide was necessary and distinct enough to displace Knudsen or either physiologist, and what the supplied evidence says about Habener.
Whether the committee prefers the physiological discovery strand, the drug-development strand, or a prize that credits both under one citation.
How much weight the absence of Eshhar from the CAR-T credit list should carry if B035 becomes the fallback.
Whether a methods advance with mainly research-tool impact (B033) meets the criterion as strongly as a therapy, and how to select three of six credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow, and I have co-authored around twenty works with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, but none of the shortlisted candidates is connected to Greengard or to that work. I am also a neurologist and chair, and I have tried to weigh optogenetics under the shared criteria and not by familiarity.
